t: Impressionist painters worked in the open air to catch the passing effects of sunlight, laying short, broken strokes of pure colour side by side instead of the smooth, blended finish the Académie demanded.
Shut out by the Salon jury, they founded their own society in December 1873 and held eight independent exhibitions from 1874 to 1886; a critic’s mocking review of the first gave them their name.
First met with harsh opposition, the style gradually won public acceptance and opened the way to Post-Impressionism, Fauvism and Cubism, with echoes in music, literature, sculpture and film.
dyk: The name came from a joke: in a satirical review of the 1874 exhibition in Le Charivari, the critic Louis Leroy played on the title of Claude Monet’s Impression, Sunrise and wrote that wallpaper in its embryonic state was more finished than that seascape.
ev: The Salon jury rejects Édouard Manet’s Le déjeuner sur l’herbe, and Napoleon III allows a Salon des Refusés, which draws more visitors than the Salon
Frédéric Bazille dies in the Franco-Prussian War
Monet, Renoir, Pissarro, Sisley, Cézanne, Morisot, Degas and others found a society to exhibit their work independently
Thirty artists show at the first exhibition in Nadar’s studio, and Louis Leroy’s review gives the group its name
Edgar Degas’s Little Dancer of Fourteen Years, his only sculpture shown in his lifetime, appears at the sixth exhibition
The seventh exhibition, the most selective, shows only nine “true” Impressionists
The group divides over the invitations to Paul Signac and Georges Seurat at the eighth and last exhibition

f.where: France, above all Paris, its cafés, boulevards and the studio of the photographer Nadar, and the countryside where the painters worked in the open air; later shown in London and New York and taken up across Europe, the Americas, Australia and Japan
f.period: the core painters meet in the early 1860s; Salon des Refusés 1863; Société anonyme founded December 1873; first exhibition April 1874; eight group exhibitions 1874–1886; Post-Impressionism from the 1880s
f.figures: Claude Monet, the most prolific and stereotypical Impressionist; Pierre-Auguste Renoir; Alfred Sisley; Camille Pissarro, the only one to show at all eight exhibitions; Berthe Morisot; Edgar Degas, who despised the term; Paul Cézanne; Mary Cassatt; Gustave Caillebotte; Édouard Manet, regarded as their leader though he never exhibited with them
f.outcome: few financial rewards from the exhibitions, but gradual public acceptance; by the early 1880s diluted Impressionist methods were commonplace in Salon art, and the movement became a precursor of Post-Impressionism, Fauvism and Cubism
